teaser.text: Verizon sells the connections that let people use phones, get online at home, and keep businesses communicating. To understand its business, follow what it sells, where a dollar comes from, and what Verizon must spend to deliver it.

stock.opening: Verizon’s weighted forecast reaches $56.40 by October 2029, hinging on durable service growth, customer retention, productive broadband investment and debt reduction. The investment works if Verizon turns network scale and Frontier’s fiber into cash while reducing debt.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Verizon’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Verizon’s shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: Verizon’s weighted value rises to $44.04 in October 2027, $49.68 in October 2028 and $56.40 in October 2029, equivalent to returns of 10%, 30% and 52% including dividends. The range is wide: by October 2029, the bear case reaches $21.88 while the bull case reaches $93.57, against today’s $42.78.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Verizon?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA is the central operating assumption. The base case rises from $53,306 million in October 2027 to $55,171 million and then $57,102 million, or growth of 3.0% followed by 3.5% annually. That exceeds the 2021–2025 historical compound growth of about 0.8%, but remains below the latest quarterly growth of 7.2%. Service revenue guidance, improved additions and Frontier’s expected savings support the base path, while debt and network investment limit margin expansion.

The bear case falls to $49,423 million before recovering slowly to $49,670 million and $50,167 million. Falling ARPA, flat wireless-service guidance and slower fixed-wireless additions justify the initial decline. The bull case reaches $54,858 million, $58,150 million and $61,639 million on sustained 6% growth, requiring lower churn, successful broadband conversion and timely Frontier savings.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Verizon really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash was $37,137 million in 2025. After capital spending including wireless licences of $17,461 million, free cash flow was $19,676 million. Subtracting $815 million of stock compensation gives analytical “real free cash flow” of $18,861 million. Employees receive shares instead of cash, but existing shareholders bear dilution.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Verizon today?

paragraphs.text: At **$42.78**, the shares value Verizon at about **$178 billion**. Its trailing P/E, or price divided by recent earnings per share, is **11.1x**. The forward P/E is **8.2x**, but that cheaper figure depends on expected earnings rather than money already earned.

blocks.heading: How much does Verizon pay its shareholders?

paragraphs.text: Dividends are $2.83 per share in the first period for all cases because the current quarterly rate is $0.7075. The base case then rises to $2.90 and $2.97, matching approximately 2.5% annual increases and the company’s long record of increases. The bear case freezes at $2.83 because debt and investment compete for cash; the bull case reaches $2.97 and $3.11 because stronger cash generation supports approximately 5% increases.

blocks.heading: Is Verizon's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: The position improved unevenly. By 2025, free cash flow reached $19,676 million, while dividends were $11,481 million. Verizon had cash left after payouts, and it made no share repurchases during these five years. In 2025, gross debt rose even as broader net debt edged down because cash and short-term investments also increased.

Operating cash was $37,137 million in 2025. After capital spending including wireless licences of $17,461 million, free cash flow was $19,676 million. Subtracting $815 million of stock compensation gives analytical “real free cash flow” of $18,861 million. Employees receive shares instead of cash, but existing shareholders bear dilution.

blocks.heading: Did Verizon keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The earlier 2023–2025 cycle shows why the rules deserve attention. Adjusted cumulative free cash flow was US$55.7 billion against a US$57.0 billion target. The relevant portion still vested at 98%, because the payout curve already awarded 90% at an earlier threshold and rose toward the target. Other measures brought the overall PSU payout to 78%.

blocks.heading: What has Verizon's revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: Revenue fell year over year, while mobility and broadband service revenue rose 2.8%. Equipment revenue fell nearly 20% as customers kept phones longer and Verizon reduced subsidies. Gross margin rose from 59.8% to 61.8%, showing how fewer handset sales can improve the mix.

Operating income fell from $8,172 million to $7,179 million. The main distortion was a $746 million pre-tax disposal loss on the international wireline business intended for the BT joint venture; after tax, the cost was $775 million. Removing it would raise net income to $4,610 million and EPS to $1.11, but profit would still be down 7.9%.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Verizon's next results?

paragraphs.text: The October 26, 2026 earnings report will test service growth, churn, promotions, cash and debt. Verizon targets its leverage range during 2027. Frontier must deliver more than $1 billion of annual operating-cost savings by 2028, alongside subscriber take-up and controlled construction costs.
